events.n: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji
events.line: The ninth Guru is recognised at Baba Bakala.
events.a: This day marks the Guruship of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, the ninth Guru. Before his Joti Jot in Delhi, Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji said only that the next Guru would be found at Bakala, and many claimants set themselves up there. The trader Bhai Makhan Shah Lubana, who had vowed an offering when his ship was in danger, recognised the true Guru in the quiet, meditative Tegh Bahadur Ji. The Guru went on to travel widely, founded Chakk Nanaki, which grew into Anandpur Sahib, and added bani to the Guru's scripture. Sangats gather for kirtan, katha and Ardas, above all at Baba Bakala Sahib.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
events.line: The Bal Guru, who served the sick of Delhi.
events.a: Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji, the eighth Guru, became Guru as a young child and is remembered as the Bal Guru. Summoned to Delhi by the emperor Aurangzeb, he stayed at the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh, where Gurdwara Bangla Sahib now stands. When smallpox and cholera spread through the city, the Guru served the sick without regard to their faith, and he himself fell ill. Before his Joti Jot he indicated that the next Guru would be found at Bakala. Sikhs remember his compassion with kirtan, katha and Ardas, especially at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib and Gurdwara Bala Sahib in Delhi, where many come to pray for the sick.

events.n: Puranmashi
Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji
events.line: The birth of the ninth Guru, in Amritsar.
events.a: Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, the ninth Guru, was born in Amritsar, the youngest son of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji and Mata Nanaki Ji. Named Tyag Mal as a child, he showed such courage in the battle of Kartarpur that he became known as Tegh Bahadur, brave of the sword. He spent many years in meditation at Bakala before the Guruship, and later travelled through Punjab, the east and Assam. His shabads and saloks in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji are treasured for their call to steadiness and detachment. The day is marked with Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, especially at Gurdwara Guru Ke Mahal in Amritsar.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Sahibzada Baba Jujhar Singh Ji
Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
events.line: The birth of the fifth Guru, at Goindwal Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the fifth Guru, was born at Goindwal Sahib to Sri Guru Ram Das Ji and Bibi Bhani Ji. As Guru he completed Sri Harmandir Sahib in the sarovar at Amritsar, with doors open on every side, and compiled the Adi Granth, installing it there in 1604. His own bani is the largest single contribution to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and includes Sukhmani Sahib. He also founded the towns of Tarn Taran and Kartarpur near Jalandhar, and encouraged Sikhs to give dasvandh, a tenth of their earnings. Sangats celebrate with Akhand Paath, kirtan and langar, and many recite Sukhmani Sahib on the day.

events.n: Sikh Dastaar Divas / World Sikh Turban Day
Khalsa Saajna Divas / Vaisakhi – Creation of Khalsa Panth
events.line: The creation of the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib, 1699.
events.a: Vaisakhi marks the day in 1699 when Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji gathered the sangat at Anandpur Sahib and created the Khalsa. The Guru asked who would give their head for the faith. Five Sikhs from different castes and regions came forward one by one and became the Panj Pyare, the five beloved ones. They received Khande di Pahul, Amrit prepared with a double-edged sword, and the Guru then asked them to give Amrit to him in turn. The Khalsa was given a distinct form, the five Ks, and a life of equality, discipline and courage. Sikhs mark the day with Nagar Kirtan, Amrit Sanchar, kirtan and langar.

events.n: Sangrand
Masya
Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji
events.line: The birth of Bhai Lehna, who became the second Guru.
events.a: Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji, the second Guru, was born Bhai Lehna at Matte di Sarai, near today's Sri Muktsar Sahib. A devotee of the goddess Durga, he met Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji at Kartarpur and stayed to serve him, and Guru Nanak Dev Ji chose him as successor over his own sons. At Khadur Sahib, Guru Angad Dev Ji gave shape to the Gurmukhi script, taught children to read it, and encouraged wrestling and good health, while Mata Khivi Ji ran the langar for all. His saloks are included in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. Sangats gather at Khadur Sahib and gurdwaras everywhere for kirtan and langar.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Bhagat Dhanna Ji
Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Ji
events.line: The birth of the third Guru, at Basarke.
events.a: Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, the third Guru, was born at Basarke. He came to Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji late in life and served him with great humility, carrying water from the river Beas before dawn, and became Guru in his seventies. At Goindwal Sahib he built the baoli, a step-well, and made langar a principle: all who came sat and ate together before meeting the Guru. He organised the sangats into manjis for preaching, spoke against sati and purdah, and appointed women among his preachers. He composed Anand Sahib, one of the banis of Nitnem. The day is marked with kirtan, Akhand Paath and langar.

events.n: Puranmashi

Birth anniversary – Sardar Jassa Singh Ahluwalia
Shaheedi Saka Paonta Sahib
events.line: Remembering the sangat killed at Gurdwara Paonta Sahib.
events.a: Gurdwara Sri Paonta Sahib stands on the banks of the Yamuna in Himachal Pradesh, where Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji lived for about four years, composed bani and gathered poets and scholars at his court. The Shaheedi Saka Paonta Sahib remembers the Sikhs who were killed in police firing at the gurdwara in 1964, during a dispute over its management and maryada. The SGPC's calendar keeps the day so that their sacrifice is not forgotten. It is observed with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas for those who gave their lives, at Paonta Sahib and in gurdwaras elsewhere, and is a day to remember the sangat's care for the Guru's places.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale
Akal Takht Sahib Ghallughara / martyrdoms of 1984
events.line: The army operation at Sri Harmandir Sahib, June 1984.
events.a: In June 1984 the Indian Army entered the complex of Sri Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, in an operation that also struck dozens of other gurdwaras across Punjab. It came during the shaheedi gurpurab of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, when the complex was full of pilgrims. Sri Akal Takht Sahib was heavily damaged, the Sikh Reference Library was destroyed, and many people lost their lives, among them pilgrims, sevadars and those who fought. Sikhs remember it as the Third Ghallughara, a great massacre. The anniversary is observed with Akhand Paath and Ardas at Sri Akal Takht Sahib, and with remembrance in gurdwaras around the world.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Bhai Mohkam Singh Ji
Shaheedi – Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale & Bhai Amrik Singh Ji
events.line: Remembered by the SGPC calendar, June 1984.
events.a: Sant Jarnail Singh Ji Khalsa Bhindranwale was the head of the Damdami Taksal, a seminary of Sikh learning, from 1977. He became widely known as a preacher who urged Sikhs to take Amrit and give up intoxicants, and later as a leading figure in the political struggle of the early 1980s. He was killed at Sri Akal Takht Sahib during the army operation of June 1984, together with Bhai Amrik Singh Ji, president of the All India Sikh Students Federation. Views of his role differ widely; the SGPC's calendar marks the day as a shaheedi. It is observed with Akhand Paath and Ardas, especially at Sri Akal Takht Sahib.

events.n: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
events.line: The sixth Guru takes up the two swords of Miri and Piri.
events.a: Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji became the sixth Guru while still a boy, after the shaheedi of his father, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji. At his Gurgaddi he wore two swords, Miri and Piri, one for worldly authority and one for spiritual authority, and taught that a Sikh must be ready to defend the oppressed as well as to pray. He built Sri Akal Takht Sahib facing Sri Harmandir Sahib, kept horses and armed Sikhs, and was held for a time in the fort of Gwalior. The day is observed with kirtan, Akhand Paath and Ardas, and many gurdwaras hold katha on the meaning of Miri and Piri.

events.n: Masya
Sangrand
Birth anniversary – Bhai Sahib Singh Ji
Shaheedi Purab – Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
events.line: The first Sikh Guru to be martyred, Lahore, 1606.
events.a: Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji, the fifth Guru, was the first Sikh Guru to be martyred. In 1606, on the orders of the emperor Jahangir, he was arrested and taken to Lahore, where he was tortured over several days: made to sit on a hot iron plate, with burning sand poured over him. He bore it in calm acceptance of the Divine Will. His body was taken to the river Ravi, where Gurdwara Dera Sahib now stands. Because the shaheedi came in the heat of summer, Sikhs everywhere set up chhabeels, serving cold sweetened water to passers-by of every faith, along with kirtan, Akhand Paath and Sukhmani Sahib.

events.n: Shaheedi – Baba Banda Singh Bahadur Ji
events.line: The Khalsa general put to death in Delhi, 1716.
events.a: Baba Banda Singh Bahadur was an ascetic at Nanded who became a Sikh on meeting Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji in 1708 and was sent to Punjab. Leading the Khalsa, he won the battle of Chappar Chiri and took Sirhind in 1710, set up Sikh rule from Lohgarh, struck coins in the name of the Gurus and gave land to those who tilled it. In 1715 he was captured at Gurdas Nangal and taken to Delhi with hundreds of Sikhs, who were executed for refusing to give up their faith. In June 1716 he was put to death after cruel torture. Gurdwaras hold kirtan and Ardas in his memory.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Bhagat Kabir Ji
Puranmashi
Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji
events.line: The birth of the sixth Guru, at Guru Ki Wadali.
events.a: Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, the sixth Guru, was born at Guru Ki Wadali near Amritsar, the only son of Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji and Mata Ganga Ji. Sikh tradition remembers attempts on his life as a child, from which he was protected. As Guru he gave the Sikhs the twin ideals of Miri and Piri, built Sri Akal Takht Sahib and led the Sikhs in battles of defence. Released from the fort of Gwalior, he secured the freedom of fifty-two imprisoned kings with him, remembered at Bandi Chhor Divas. He founded Kiratpur Sahib. The day is celebrated with kirtan and langar, especially at Gurdwara Guru Ki Wadali.

events.n: Foundation Stone / Sirjana Divas – Sri Akal Takht Sahib
Foundation Stone of Sachkhand Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar
Shaheedi Purab – Bhai Mani Singh Ji
events.line: The scholar and granthi who would not give up his faith.
events.a: Bhai Mani Singh Ji was a lifelong companion of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and is remembered as the scribe who wrote out Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Damdama Sahib as the Guru dictated. After the Guru, he served as granthi of Sri Harmandir Sahib. When he sought leave for Sikhs to gather at Amritsar for Diwali, the governor of Lahore demanded a tax he could not pay, and he was sentenced to death. Offered his life if he gave up his faith, he refused and was executed by being cut apart, joint by joint. Gurdwaras hold kirtan, katha and Ardas in his memory.

events.n: Masya
Sangrand
Shaheedi Purab – Bhai Taru Singh Ji
events.line: He kept his kes, and gave his life, Lahore, 1745.
events.a: Bhai Taru Singh Ji was a young farmer of Poohla village, near Amritsar, who shared what he grew with the Sikhs living in the forests to escape persecution. In 1745 he was arrested and brought before the governor of Lahore, who offered him his life if he would cut his kes and leave the Sikh faith. He refused, and his scalp was removed. He bore it with calm and is remembered as an example of devotion to the kes, the uncut hair that the Gurus gave the Sikhs as part of their form. Sikhs remember him with kirtan, katha and Ardas on the day.

events.n: Miri-Piri Divas – Sixth Patshahi
Puranmashi
Shaheedi – Sardar Udham Singh Ji
events.line: Hanged in London, 1940, remembering Jallianwala Bagh.
events.a: Sardar Udham Singh, brought up in the Central Khalsa Orphanage in Amritsar, never forgot the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of April 1919, when British troops fired on a peaceful gathering and killed hundreds. In March 1940, in London, he shot Sir Michael O'Dwyer, who had been Lieutenant Governor of Punjab at the time of the massacre. He was tried and hanged at Pentonville Prison on 31 July 1940. In 1974 his remains were brought back to India and cremated at his home town of Sunam. He is remembered as a shaheed of the freedom struggle, with tributes, Ardas and gatherings across Punjab, above all at Sunam.

events.n: Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
events.line: The birth of the eighth Guru, at Kiratpur Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji, the eighth Guru, was born at Kiratpur Sahib to Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji and Mata Kishan Kaur Ji. He was given the Guruship as a young child, ahead of his elder brother Ram Rai, and is remembered as the Bal Guru, the child Guru. Despite his years he was known for his wisdom, gentleness and composure. During his stay in Delhi he cared for those stricken by an epidemic, and the water of the sarovar at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib is still taken home by many as a blessing. Sangats mark his Prakash Purab with kirtan, Akhand Paath and langar.

Ardas Day for Punjabis killed during the 1947 Partition
Sangrand
Shaheedi – Sant Harchand Singh Ji Longowal
events.line: The Akali leader killed in 1985, weeks after the Punjab accord.
events.a: Sant Harchand Singh Ji Longowal was a preacher and kirtani from the village of Longowal in Sangrur district who rose to lead the Shiromani Akali Dal. He led the Dharam Yudh Morcha of the early 1980s, and was among the Akali leaders detained after June 1984. In July 1985 he signed an accord with Prime Minister Rajiv Gandhi that was meant to settle Punjab's long-standing demands. Less than a month later he was shot dead while addressing a gathering at a gurdwara in Sherpur, near Sangrur. The SGPC's calendar keeps his shaheedi, and it is observed with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, especially at Longowal.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Bhai Daya Singh Ji
Jorh Mela – Baba Bakala Sahib / Guru Ladho Re
Puranmashi
Sampuranta Divas – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji at Sri Harmandir Sahib
Masya
First Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (1604)
events.line: The Adi Granth is first installed at Sri Harmandir Sahib, 1604.
events.a: In 1604 Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji completed the compilation of the Adi Granth, bringing together the bani of the first five Gurus with that of Bhagats and saints of many backgrounds, written out by Bhai Gurdas Ji at Ramsar in Amritsar. It was installed for the first time in Sri Harmandir Sahib, with Baba Budha Ji as the first granthi, and the Guru himself is remembered as giving it the place of honour. This day, the Pehla Prakash Purab, celebrates that first installation. Sangats hold Akhand Paath, kirtan and Nagar Kirtan, and Sri Harmandir Sahib is lit and decorated for the day.

events.n: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji
events.line: The fifth Guru receives the Guruship at Goindwal Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji became the fifth Guru when his father, Sri Guru Ram Das Ji, entrusted him with the Guruship at Goindwal Sahib shortly before his own Joti Jot. Tradition remembers the letters of longing the young Arjan Dev Ji sent to his father while away in Lahore, which showed the depth of his devotion. His Guruship was opposed by his elder brother, Prithi Chand, but he met that hostility with patience. Over the next quarter of a century he completed Sri Harmandir Sahib, compiled the Adi Granth and gave the Sikhs a strong, organised community. The day is marked with kirtan and Ardas in gurdwaras.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
events.line: The fourth Guru, founder of Amritsar.
events.a: Sri Guru Ram Das Ji, the fourth Guru, completed his life on earth at Goindwal Sahib, after entrusting the Guruship to his youngest son, Sri Guru Arjan Dev Ji. As Guru he founded the town first called Ramdaspur, now Amritsar, had its sarovar dug, and invited traders and craftsmen of many kinds to settle there, so that the town would support itself. His bani in Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji includes the Laavan, the four hymns at the heart of the Anand Karaj, the Sikh wedding. Sangats remember him on this day with kirtan, katha and Ardas at Goindwal Sahib, at Amritsar and in gurdwaras everywhere.

events.n: Sangrand
Jorh Mela Gurdwara Kandh Sahib / Marriage of Guru Nanak Dev Ji
Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
events.line: Bhai Jetha Ji becomes the fourth Guru.
events.a: Bhai Jetha Ji, born in Lahore and orphaned young, came to Goindwal Sahib and served Sri Guru Amar Das Ji with total humility, carrying earth and water for the building of the baoli. He married the Guru's daughter, Bibi Bhani Ji, and was chosen above the Guru's own sons to become the fourth Guru, Sri Guru Ram Das Ji. Sikh tradition tells of a test in which platforms were built and pulled down again and again at the Guru's word; only Bhai Jetha Ji kept rebuilding without complaint. The day of his Gurgaddi is celebrated with kirtan and Ardas at Goindwal Sahib, Amritsar and gurdwaras around the world.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Ji / Goindwal Sahib Jorh Mela
events.line: With the Jorh Mela at Goindwal Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Amar Das Ji, the third Guru, completed his life on earth at Goindwal Sahib in his nineties, having entrusted the Guruship to Sri Guru Ram Das Ji. In more than two decades as Guru he made Goindwal Sahib a centre of the Sikh faith, built its baoli of eighty-four steps, and made langar a practice in which everyone sits together as an equal. He composed Anand Sahib, one of the banis of Nitnem. The day is marked by a Jorh Mela at Goindwal Sahib, where pilgrims recite Japji Sahib on the steps of the baoli and bathe in it, and by kirtan and Ardas everywhere.

events.n: Puranmashi
Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji
events.line: Guru Nanak Dev Ji names Bhai Lehna as Guru Angad.
events.a: At Kartarpur, on the banks of the Ravi, Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji chose Bhai Lehna Ji as his successor, having tested his devotion again and again over years of service. Guru Nanak Dev Ji placed a coconut and five paise before him, bowed to him, and named him Angad, a part of his own body. Passing over his own sons, he showed that the Guruship would go by devotion and service, not by birth. Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji then moved to Khadur Sahib to carry the Guru's work forward. The day is celebrated with kirtan and Ardas at Khadur Sahib, at Kartarpur Sahib and in gurdwaras everywhere.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
events.line: The founder of the Sikh faith, at Kartarpur.
events.a: Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of the Sikh faith, spent his last years at Kartarpur, the town he founded on the Ravi, farming the land and leading the sangat in kirtan and langar. Before completing his life on earth he passed the Guruship to Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji. Sikh tradition remembers that his Hindu and Muslim followers each wished to perform his last rites in their own way, and that when the sheet over his body was lifted only flowers were found. Gurdwara Darbar Sahib Kartarpur, now in Pakistan, marks the place. Sangats remember the day with kirtan, katha and Ardas, in Punjab and around the world.

Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Ram Das Sahib Ji
events.line: The birth of the fourth Guru, founder of Amritsar.
events.a: Sri Guru Ram Das Ji, the fourth Guru, was born Bhai Jetha Ji in Chuna Mandi, Lahore. Orphaned as a child, he earned his living selling boiled grain, and came to Goindwal Sahib, where his humble service to Sri Guru Amar Das Ji led to the Guruship. He founded the town of Ramdaspur, now Amritsar, and had the sarovar dug around which Sri Harmandir Sahib would later rise. His bani includes the Laavan of the Anand Karaj. The day is celebrated with great joy in Amritsar, where Sri Harmandir Sahib is lit up and Nagar Kirtan fills the streets, and with kirtan, Akhand Paath and langar in gurdwaras everywhere.

events.n: Shaheedi – Bhai Beant Singh Ji
events.line: Marked in the SGPC calendar; October 1984.
events.a: Bhai Beant Singh was a member of the security staff of Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. On 31 October 1984, months after the army operation at Sri Harmandir Sahib, he and another guard, Satwant Singh, shot the Prime Minister at her residence in New Delhi. He was killed in custody the same day. The assassination was followed by days of mass killings of Sikhs in Delhi and other cities. Views of the act differ sharply; the SGPC's calendar marks his death as a shaheedi, and the day is observed with Ardas at Sri Akal Takht Sahib. Many Sikhs also use these days to remember the innocent people killed in November 1984.

events.n: Punjabi Suba Day
Birth anniversary – Mata Sahib Kaur Ji
Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji
events.line: The youngest of the Gurus receives the Guruship.
events.a: Before his Joti Jot at Kiratpur Sahib, Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji entrusted the Guruship to his younger son, Harkrishan Ji, then a small child, rather than to his elder son, Ram Rai, who had displeased him at the Mughal court. Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji thus became the eighth Guru, and the youngest. His Guruship was short, lasting only a few years, but he is remembered for a calm wisdom beyond his years and for his care of the sick in Delhi. The day is marked with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Kiratpur Sahib and at Gurdwara Bangla Sahib in Delhi.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji
events.line: The gentle seventh Guru, at Kiratpur Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji, the seventh Guru, completed his life on earth at Kiratpur Sahib after entrusting the Guruship to his young son, Sri Guru Harkrishan Sahib Ji. A grandson of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, he was known for his gentleness and his love of nature. He kept gardens and a dispensary of herbal medicines at Kiratpur Sahib and, by tradition, sent medicine that healed a son of the emperor Shah Jahan. He kept a large body of mounted Sikhs, yet his Guruship was largely peaceful, given to preaching. Sikhs remember him with kirtan and Ardas, at Kiratpur Sahib and in gurdwaras everywhere.

events.n: Bandi Chhor Divas / Diwali
events.line: Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji returns from Gwalior.
events.a: Bandi Chhor Divas, the Day of Liberation, falls with Diwali. It remembers the release of Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji from the fort of Gwalior, where he had been held by the emperor Jahangir. When the Guru was told he was free to go, he refused to leave without the fifty-two kings imprisoned with him. He was allowed to take out as many as could hold on to his cloak, and he had a cloak made with fifty-two tassels so that all walked free. His return to Amritsar was greeted with lamps. Sikhs light Sri Harmandir Sahib and their homes, and hold kirtan, Ardas and fireworks over the sarovar.

events.n: Masya
Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji (Nanded, 1708)
events.line: The Guruship is passed to the Granth at Nanded, 1708.
events.a: In 1708 at Nanded, on the banks of the Godavari, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji ended the line of human Gurus and conferred the Guruship on Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji, the scripture he had completed by adding the bani of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji. From that day Sikhs have bowed to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji as their living Guru, the eternal presence of the Guru in the Word, with the Guru Khalsa Panth guided by it. The day is celebrated as Gurta Gaddi Divas with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Nagar Kirtan, above all at Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib in Nanded.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
events.line: The tenth Guru, at Nanded, 1708.
events.a: Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, the tenth Guru, completed his life on earth at Nanded in 1708, some weeks after he was wounded by an assassin. Before his Joti Jot he passed the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji and to the Guru Khalsa Panth, so that no human Guru would follow him. In the years before, he had lost his father, his mother and all four of his sons, yet he remained steadfast and without bitterness, and continued to lead the Panth. Takht Sachkhand Sri Hazur Sahib stands at the place. The day is marked with kirtan, katha and Ardas around the world.

events.n: Shaheedi Purab – Baba Deep Singh Ji
events.line: He set out to free Sri Harmandir Sahib, 1757.
events.a: Baba Deep Singh Ji took Amrit from Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji and later stayed at Damdama Sahib, where he made copies of Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji by hand. He led the Shaheedan Misl. In 1757, already in his seventies, he set out to free Sri Harmandir Sahib after it had been desecrated by the forces of Ahmad Shah Abdali, and many Singhs joined him on the way. He fell in battle near Amritsar, and Sikh tradition remembers him fighting on to reach the sacred precincts. Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Baba Deep Singh Ji in Amritsar marks the place, and sangats gather there for kirtan and Ardas on the day.

events.n: Foundation Day – SGPC
Sangrand
Shaheedi – Sardar Kartar Singh Sarabha Ji
events.line: The young Ghadar revolutionary, hanged in Lahore, 1915.
events.a: Kartar Singh Sarabha, from the village of Sarabha near Ludhiana, went to study in the United States as a teenager and joined the Ghadar Party, formed by Indians abroad, many of them Punjabi Sikhs, to end British rule in India. He helped produce its newspaper and returned to India in 1914 to prepare an uprising. The plan was betrayed, and he was arrested and tried in the first Lahore Conspiracy Case. He was hanged in Lahore in November 1915, still a teenager. Bhagat Singh later spoke of him as an inspiration. He is remembered with tributes, Ardas and gatherings, above all in his village of Sarabha.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Bhagat Namdev Ji
Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji
events.line: The birth of the founder of the Sikh faith, 1469.
events.a: Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, the founder of the Sikh faith, was born in 1469 at Rai Bhoi di Talwandi, now Nankana Sahib in Pakistan, to Mehta Kalu Ji and Mata Tripta Ji. He taught devotion to the one Creator, honest work, sharing with others and the equality of all people. For many years he travelled on long journeys, the udasis, with Bhai Mardana Ji, and later settled at Kartarpur. His Prakash Purab is the most widely celebrated Gurpurab. It falls on the full moon of Katak and is marked with Akhand Paath, Prabhat Pheris at dawn, Nagar Kirtan, illuminated gurdwaras and langar for all.

events.n: Puranmashi
Akāl Chāṇā / Merging of Bhai Mardana Ji
events.line: The rababi who travelled with Guru Nanak Dev Ji.
events.a: Bhai Mardana Ji was a Muslim minstrel from Talwandi, the village of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji's birth, and his companion for most of his life. On the long journeys of the udasis he played the rabab while the Guru sang the bani, and he is remembered as the first of the Guru's rababis and a forerunner of the Sikh kirtan tradition. Sikh tradition holds that the Guru gave him a place of honour and close friendship. This day remembers his passing, his merging with the Divine. Sikhs remember his devotion with kirtan, often with string instruments in the old style, and with Ardas in gurdwaras.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Sahibzada Baba Zorawar Singh Ji
Shaheedi – Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji
events.line: Thirty Singhs who defended Sri Harmandir Sahib, 1764.
events.a: Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji was a Nihang Singh of the eighteenth century who took Amrit as a young man and served the Panth all his life. In 1764, when Ahmad Shah Abdali's army advanced on Amritsar, most of the Khalsa were away. He chose to stay with about thirty Singhs to defend Sri Harmandir Sahib, though they knew they could not win. They prepared with Ardas and met the invading army at the gates, fighting until every one of them fell. Gurdwara Shaheed Ganj Baba Gurbakhsh Singh Ji, behind Sri Akal Takht Sahib, marks the place, and sangats remember them there with kirtan and Ardas.

events.n: Masya
Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
events.line: The tenth Guru, at Anandpur Sahib, aged nine.
events.a: Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji became the tenth Guru at Anandpur Sahib when he was a boy of nine, after his father, Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, gave his life in Delhi. Sikh tradition remembers that the young Gobind Rai encouraged his father to go to Delhi and stand for the Kashmiri Pandits who had come to him for help. As Guru he went on to create the Khalsa, write a large body of bani and poetry, and at the end pass the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. The day is marked with kirtan, katha and Ardas, especially at Takht Sri Kesgarh Sahib in Anandpur Sahib.

events.n: Shaheedi – Bhai Dyala Ji, Bhai Mati Das Ji & Bhai Sati Das Ji
events.line: Three Sikhs martyred before Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji, 1675.
events.a: In Delhi in 1675 three Sikhs who had been arrested with Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji were put to death in front of him, to make him give up his stand. Bhai Mati Das Ji and Bhai Sati Das Ji were brothers. Bhai Mati Das Ji was sawn in two, Bhai Sati Das Ji was wrapped in cotton and burnt, and Bhai Dyala Ji was boiled in a cauldron. Each remained calm, in remembrance of the Divine, to the end. Their shaheedi came shortly before the Guru's own, at Chandni Chowk. Sikhs remember all three with kirtan and Ardas, especially at Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib in Delhi.

events.n: Birth anniversary – Sahibzada Baba Fateh Singh Ji
Guruship conferred to Panj Pyare / Guru Khalsa at Chamkaur Sahib
events.line: The Panj Pyare ask the Guru to leave the garhi.
events.a: At Chamkaur Sahib, after his two elder sons had fallen in battle, Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji was asked by the few Singhs still with him to leave the garhi, so that he could live to lead the Panth. Five Singhs, standing as the Panj Pyare, gave him this instruction as the Khalsa, and the Guru accepted it, honouring the Khalsa as his own form. The day is remembered as the time the Guru placed his authority in the Guru Khalsa, the five acting together. He left that night, and the remaining Singhs fought on. Gurdwaras at Chamkaur Sahib hold kirtan, katha and Ardas to remember the day.

events.n: Shaheedi Purab – Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji
events.line: Hind di Chadar, martyred in Delhi, 1675.
events.a: In 1675 Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji gave his life in Delhi for the freedom of others to follow their own faith. Kashmiri Pandits facing forced conversion had come to him at Anandpur Sahib for help, and he chose to go to Delhi and stand for them. Held on the orders of the emperor Aurangzeb and asked to give up his faith or perform a miracle, he refused both and was beheaded at Chandni Chowk. Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib marks the place, and Gurdwara Rakab Ganj Sahib the place of his cremation. Sikhs remember him as Hind di Chadar, the shield of India, with kirtan, katha and Nagar Kirtan.

Family separation at Sirsa River
Shaheedi – Bhai Jivan Singh (Bhai Jaita Ji)
events.line: He carried the Guru's head from Delhi to Anandpur Sahib.
events.a: Bhai Jaita Ji is remembered for an act of great courage in 1675. After the shaheedi of Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji in Delhi, he took up the Guru's sacred head and carried it in secret all the way to Anandpur Sahib, where the young Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji received it with honour. He later took Amrit and became Bhai Jivan Singh Ji, a warrior and poet in the Guru's service. He gave his life in the battles that followed the leaving of Anandpur Sahib in December. Gurdwara Sis Ganj Sahib at Anandpur Sahib marks where the head was cremated, and Sikhs remember him with kirtan and Ardas.

events.n: Saka Chamkaur Sahib
Puranmashi
Shaheedi – Sahibzada Baba Ajit Singh Ji (Saka Chamkaur)
events.line: The elder Sahibzade at Saka Chamkaur.
events.a: The two elder Sahibzade, Baba Ajit Singh Ji and Baba Jujhar Singh Ji, sons of Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, gave their lives at Chamkaur Sahib in December, after the Guru and a small band of Singhs had left Anandpur Sahib. Besieged in a mud fortress, the garhi, by a far larger army, the Singhs went out in small groups to fight. Baba Ajit Singh Ji went first, and his younger brother, still a boy, asked to follow him. The Guru blessed both and watched each of them fall. Gurdwara Qatalgarh Sahib marks the place. Sangats observe the Shaheedi Jorh Mela at Chamkaur Sahib with kirtan and Ardas.

events.n: Shaheedi – Sahibzada Baba Jujhar Singh Ji (Saka Chamkaur)
Shaheedi – Bhai Sangat Singh Ji
events.line: He stayed in the garhi at Chamkaur Sahib.
events.a: Bhai Sangat Singh Ji was among the last Singhs in the garhi at Chamkaur Sahib. When the Guru Khalsa asked Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji to leave so that he could continue to lead the Panth, Bhai Sangat Singh Ji remained in the fortress in the Guru's place, so that the besieging army believed the Guru was still inside. This helped the Guru to get away under the cover of darkness. Bhai Sangat Singh Ji fell fighting the next day with the few Singhs who remained. He is remembered at Chamkaur Sahib with kirtan and Ardas, and as an example of selfless sacrifice for the Guru and the Panth.

events.n: Shaheedi – Mata Gujri Ji
Shaheedi – Sahibzada Baba Fateh Singh Ji
events.line: The younger Sahibzade and Mata Gujri Ji at Sirhind.
events.a: After the Guru's family was separated at the Sirsa river, Mata Gujri Ji and her two youngest grandsons, Baba Zorawar Singh Ji and Baba Fateh Singh Ji, were betrayed and handed to Wazir Khan, the governor of Sirhind. They were held in the Thanda Burj, a tower open to the winter wind. The Sahibzade, still children, were offered their lives if they gave up their faith; they refused, were bricked into a wall and were then put to death. Mata Gujri Ji passed away on hearing the news. Gurdwara Fatehgarh Sahib marks the place, where the Shaheedi Jorh Mela draws great sangats every year.

events.n: Shaheedi – Sahibzada Baba Zorawar Singh Ji
Masya
Sri Muktsar Sahib Jorh Mela (Maaghi)
events.line: The Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones.
events.a: Maaghi, on the first day of the month of Magh, remembers the battle of Khidrana, where forty Singhs who had earlier left Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji at Anandpur Sahib returned, led by Mai Bhago Ji, and fought a pursuing Mughal army. All forty fell. Sikh tradition remembers that the Guru found Bhai Mahan Singh still alive and, at his request, tore up the disclaimer the forty had signed, blessing them as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones. Khidrana became Sri Muktsar Sahib. A large Jorh Mela is held there each year, with a holy dip in the sarovar, kirtan and Ardas.

events.n: Sangrand
Foundation Stone of Sachkhand Sri Harmandir Sahib, Amritsar
Prakash Purab – Sri Guru Gobind Singh Sahib Ji
events.line: The birth of the tenth Guru, at Patna Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Gobind Singh Ji, the tenth Guru, was born Gobind Rai at Patna Sahib, to Sri Guru Tegh Bahadur Sahib Ji and Mata Gujri Ji, while his father was travelling in the east. He grew up at Anandpur Sahib, became Guru as a boy, and created the Khalsa in 1699. A warrior, poet and scholar, he gathered learned men around him and gave his family and his whole life for the Panth. Before his Joti Jot he passed the Guruship to Sri Guru Granth Sahib Ji. His Prakash Purab is celebrated with Nagar Kirtan, Akhand Paath and langar, above all at Takht Sri Harimandir Ji, Patna Sahib.

Wadda Ghallughara – Kup Rohira, Sangrur
events.line: The great holocaust of February 1762.
events.a: The Wadda Ghallughara, the great holocaust, took place in February 1762 near Kup Rohira, in today's Malerkotla area. The forces of Ahmad Shah Abdali surprised a large Sikh caravan that included many women, children and elderly people. The Khalsa formed a moving wall around them and fought through the whole day as they marched, but a very large number of Sikhs were killed. It is remembered as one of the darkest days in Sikh history, and yet within months the Khalsa had regained its strength. The day is observed with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, and at the memorial at Kup Rohira, where sangats gather.

Saka Nankana Sahib
events.line: The shaheeds of Gurdwara Janam Asthan, 1921.
events.a: In February 1921, at Gurdwara Janam Asthan in Nankana Sahib, the birthplace of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, a jatha of Sikhs led by Bhai Lachhman Singh Dharowali came to end the control of the mahant, who ran the shrine as his private property. The mahant's armed men attacked them, and many Sikhs were killed; Bhai Lachhman Singh Ji was tied to a tree and burnt. The saka moved the whole Panth and gave force to the Gurdwara Reform Movement, which led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925. Sangats remember the shaheeds with Akhand Paath, kirtan and Ardas, at Nankana Sahib and everywhere.

Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
events.line: The seventh Guru, chosen by his grandfather.
events.a: Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji entrusted the Guruship to his grandson, Har Rai Ji, at Kiratpur Sahib, choosing him for his gentle nature and devotion. Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji became the seventh Guru while still young. Sikh tradition tells that as a boy he once brushed against a flower with his robe and was saddened to see its petals fall, and that this shaped his tender care for every living thing. He kept a herbal dispensary at Kiratpur Sahib and travelled to preach in Punjab and beyond, while keeping a body of mounted Sikhs ready. The day is marked with kirtan and Ardas at Kiratpur Sahib and elsewhere.

events.n: Gurgaddi Purab – Sri Guru Amar Das Sahib Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
events.line: The third Guru, after years of service.
events.a: Sri Guru Amar Das Ji became the third Guru at Khadur Sahib, chosen by Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji after many years of selfless service. Already an old man, he would rise before dawn to carry water from the river Beas for the Guru. Sikh tradition tells of a stormy night when he stumbled near a weaver's hut and was mocked as a man with no home, and how the Guru then honoured him as the home of the homeless. He went on to make Goindwal Sahib the centre of the Sikh faith. The day is marked with kirtan and Ardas at Khadur Sahib and Goindwal Sahib.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
events.line: The second Guru, at Khadur Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Angad Dev Ji, the second Guru, completed his life on earth at Khadur Sahib after passing the Guruship to Sri Guru Amar Das Ji. In thirteen years as Guru he gave the Sikhs much of their early shape: he developed and spread the Gurmukhi script, gathered the hymns of Sri Guru Nanak Dev Ji, opened schools for children and, with Mata Khivi Ji, made langar a daily feature of Khadur Sahib. He encouraged physical fitness and wrestling among the young. Sangats gather for kirtan and Ardas at Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Khadur Sahib, and in gurdwaras everywhere, to remember his life of service.

events.n: Joti Jot Purab – Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji (fixed solar anniversary)
events.line: The sixth Guru, at Kiratpur Sahib.
events.a: Sri Guru Hargobind Sahib Ji, the sixth Guru, completed his life on earth at Kiratpur Sahib, on the banks of the Sutlej, where he spent his last years. His Guruship, the longest of the ten Gurus, saw the Sikhs take up arms in defence, the building of Sri Akal Takht Sahib, and his release from the fort of Gwalior together with fifty-two kings. Before his Joti Jot he passed the Guruship to his grandson, Sri Guru Har Rai Sahib Ji. Gurdwara Patalpuri Sahib at Kiratpur Sahib, where his last rites took place, is visited by many. Sangats hold kirtan and Ardas on the day.
